I couldn't answer this properly. My search tool only shows which filings contain the search terms, not the text itself, so I can't tell you what US Steel actually said about the Nippon Steel merger or how it affects operations. **Not found with these tools:** the merger and risk-factor sections of US Steel's filings. (The ticker "X" also didn't work in most tools, so I searched by company name. I took "Nippton" to mean Nippon Steel.) I've now used my budget of about eight tool calls.

**What the searches do show (as of 16 May 2025):**

1. **Annual and quarterly reports.** The 2024 10-K (filed 31 Jan 2025) and the Q1 2025 10-Q (filed 2 May 2025) both mention "Nippon Steel" together with "merger agreement." Both also come up in searches about a CFIUS order blocking the merger and a related lawsuit. CFIUS is the US government committee that reviews foreign investments for national-security risk.
2. **Trump-era CFIUS review.** Three filings mention Nippon Steel, "President Trump" and CFIUS review together: an 8-K investor communication (8 Apr 2025), the Q1 2025 results materials (8-K, 1 May 2025) and the Q1 10-Q. So the company was still pursuing the deal under the new administration when it reported Q1.
3. **Shareholder communications.** Investor 8-Ks from 17 Mar and 8 Apr 2025 come up in the searches about the CFIUS order and lawsuit.
4. **Proxy fight.** A contested proxy fight was underway in spring 2025. Activist Ancora filed materials against the board (DFAN14A, PREC14A, PRRN14A, DEFC14A), and US Steel filed its own proxy (DEFC14A) and extra solicitation materials (DEFA14A). Several of these documents contain the phrases "termination fee" and "$565 million." I can't confirm from here what that fee is, who would pay it, or whether US Steel or Ancora wrote that language.
5. **SEC staff review.** In March 2025, SEC staff comment letters (UPLOAD) and US Steel's reply (CORRESP) also matched the CFIUS and termination-fee terms.

**What I couldn't confirm:** limits the merger agreement puts on how US Steel runs its business before closing, effects on employees and customers, and merger-related costs. One exact-phrase search on business restrictions found nothing, and my last search failed.

The best next step is to read the "Merger Agreement" note and the risk factors in the Q1 2025 10-Q. That filing shows up in every merger-related search above, so it is likely the most complete and current account.
